explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Job says, "my lips will not speak wickedness, and my tongue will not utter deceit." (Job 27:4) He ties it to his breath, so the promise runs as long as he's breathing. That's a promise with no expiration date, and I can't even keep a timer promise on a batch.

Close, but Job never promises to stop asking God. In this passage his promise is about wickedness and deceit: "my lips will not speak wickedness, and my tongue will not utter deceit." (Job 27:4) He's guarding what comes out of his mouth, and he says it will hold as long as breath is in him (Job 27:3). Keep an eye on what he promises NOT to say.

Nope, and Job is still answering his friends right here. He's mid-speech, and his lips are busy. What he promises is that they won't speak wickedness and his tongue won't utter deceit (Job 27:4). So he's talking, just talking clean.

Not quite, friend. Job says the opposite: "I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die." (Job 27:5) His friends have been pressing him to admit he did something to earn all this, and he isn't budging. So that's a False, and a firm one.
Right, friend. Job says, "I will never say that you are right; I will maintain my integrity until I die." (Job 27:5) No giving in, no "okay, you win." This man has dug in like dough in a cold bowl.

That's it. Job says, "As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me." (Job 27:6) He's saying his own inner voice has nothing to charge him with. For a man whose friends keep accusing him, that's a big claim.

Not this one. Job doesn't mention his memory here. He says, "As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me." (Job 27:6) It's the inner voice that stays quiet, not the remembering part. Though I'll admit my memory accuses me every time I think of that junk drawer.

Good guess, since Job is stubborn, but the text doesn't say that. He says, "As long as I live, my conscience will not accuse me." (Job 27:6) The word is conscience, that inner voice. Pride never gets named in this verse.

Yes, friend. Job asks, "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?" (Job 27:9) It's a question, and Job leaves it hanging for his friends to chew on. He follows it with more questions about the godless man in the next verse.

Not the one Job asks. His question is about God: "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?" (Job 27:9) Friends don't come up in that verse. Funny thing is, Job's own friends are the ones lecturing him right now.

Not in this verse, friend. Job asks, "Will God hear his cry when distress comes upon him?" (Job 27:9) Riches come up later in the passage, but there Job says the wicked man's silver gets divided by the innocent (Job 27:17). Right now the question is about whether God hears.

That's right. Job asks, "Will he delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?" (Job 27:10) Same man, same string of questions, one after another. Job is making his friends think about what the godless actually have.

Not this time, friend. Job really does ask it: "Will he delight in the Almighty? Will he call upon God at all times?" (Job 27:10) It comes right after the question about whether God will hear the godless man's cry. So this one is True.

That's the word. Job says, "Why then do you keep up this empty talk?" (Job 27:12) He's telling his friends they've seen it for themselves, so why all the hot air? I've heard some empty talk in my day, mostly from a coupon in a drawer that still believed in itself.
Not quite, friend. Job doesn't call it wise. He says, "Why then do you keep up this empty talk?" (Job 27:12) The word is empty, and he says it right to their faces.
Not this one. Job says, "Why then do you keep up this empty talk?" (Job 27:12) Kind isn't the word. Job is calling their talk empty, and I'd say he's not in a mood for gentle.

Not this time, friend. Job says, "Though his sons are many, they are destined for the sword; and his offspring will never have enough food." (Job 27:14) That's the opposite of long and peaceful. So this one is False.

Right. Job says, "Though his sons are many, they are destined for the sword; and his offspring will never have enough food." (Job 27:14) Lots of sons, but no long and peaceful life. A heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit.

explanations.answer: They will not weep for them
explanations.explanation: That's it. Job says, "and their widows will not weep for them." (Job 27:15) It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to sound that heavy. Nobody even stops to cry.

explanations.answer: They will mourn for many days
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Job says the opposite: "and their widows will not weep for them." (Job 27:15) No mourning at all. It's a hard verse.
Not here. Job says, "and their widows will not weep for them." (Job 27:15) Tearing clothes is never mentioned in this verse. The widows simply don't weep.

Yes, friend. Job says, "what he lays up, the righteous will wear, and his silver will be divided by the innocent." (Job 27:17) All that piling up, and somebody else ends up wearing it. That's one expensive way to dress someone else.
Not this time. Job says, "what he lays up, the righteous will wear." (Job 27:17) So the clothes he piles up go to someone else, and that makes this True. The silver gets divided too, by the innocent.

explanations.answer: A hut set up by a watchman
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Job says the house is "like a moth's cocoon, like a hut set up by a watchman." (Job 27:18) Neither one is built to last. Two pictures, same message: flimsy.

explanations.answer: A tent pitched by a shepherd
explanations.explanation: Close in feel, but not what Job says. His words are "like a hut set up by a watchman." (Job 27:18) The builder in the verse is a watchman, not a shepherd. Watch the details on that one.

explanations.answer: A shelter made by a prophet
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. Job says, "like a hut set up by a watchman." (Job 27:18) No prophets in that verse. It's a watchman's hut, a simple thing set up for a short while.

That's the word. Job says, "He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more; when he opens his eyes, all is gone." (Job 27:19) He goes to sleep with everything and wakes up with nothing. I'd be checking under the pillow.
Not quite, friend. The verse says, "He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more." (Job 27:19) Worry isn't mentioned. The point is that he's wealthy when he lies down, and by morning it's all gone.

Not this one. Job says, "He lies down wealthy, but will do so no more; when he opens his eyes, all is gone." (Job 27:19) Being alone isn't in the verse. The word is wealthy, and that's what makes the loss sting.
Yes, friend. Job says, "It hurls itself against him without mercy as he flees headlong from its power." (Job 27:22) He's running flat out, and the wind keeps coming. No softening it.
Not what Job says. The verse is "It hurls itself against him without mercy as he flees headlong from its power." (Job 27:22) No warning is mentioned. The wind just comes, and he runs.

Not here, friend. Job says it hurls itself "without mercy" while the man flees headlong (Job 27:22). Nothing in the verse says it's only for a moment. The picture is of a man running with the wind on his heels.
Not quite, friend. Job says, "It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place." (Job 27:23) That's no welcome home. It's the opposite, so this one is False.
Right. Job says, "It claps its hands at him and hisses him out of his place." (Job 27:23) The wind is sending him away, not welcoming him back. That's about as warm as a cold oven.
